title: Young modulus and material stiffness
prior_knowledge_summary: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area.
Strain is extension divided by the original length.
Stress has unit Pa and strain is dimensionless.
The proportional region is represented by a straight line through the origin.
new_learning: Define Young modulus as tensile stress divided by tensile strain.
Use E = stress/strain = FL/(AΔL) within the proportional tensile region.
Interpret stress-strain gradient as Young modulus and compare material stiffness.

visual_planning.reason: Six visuals develop material comparison, ratio meaning, derivation, graph gradient, worked calculation and misconception correction.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: How can differently sized samples reveal the material itself?
content: A thick short sample and a thin long sample can show very different forces and extensions even when made from the same material. Stress removes the area effect and strain removes the original-length effect.
Comparing stress with strain gives a stiffness measure that belongs to the material in its proportional tensile region.

figure.brief: Show two differently sized samples of the same material with raw F and ΔL values, then arrows leading to matching stress-strain behaviour.
figure.alt_text: Differently sized samples are normalised using stress and strain.

blocks.title: Young modulus
blocks.accepted_definition: the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain
content: Young modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain. This definition applies to tensile behaviour in the proportional region.
Stress is measured in Pa and strain has no unit, so Young modulus also has unit Pa. A larger E means more stress is required to produce the same strain, so the material is stiffer.

figure.brief: Stress-over-strain fraction beside two equal-strain samples requiring small and large stress; label the larger ratio as stiffer.
figure.alt_text: A larger stress-to-strain ratio represents a stiffer material.

blocks.title: Connect E to measured quantities
content: Start with E = stress/strain. Substitute stress = F/A and strain = ΔL/L.
E = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). Here L is original length and ΔL is extension.
This form is useful for calculation. It does not replace the meaning: Young modulus remains stress divided by strain.

figure.purpose: Show the algebra without skipped steps
figure.brief: Annotated fraction-of-fractions derivation from E = σ/ε to FL/(AΔL), with each symbol linked to a sample sketch.
figure.alt_text: The Young modulus formula is derived from stress and strain definitions.

blocks.title: Read E from a stress-strain graph
content: Plot strain horizontally and tensile stress vertically. In the proportional region the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Gradient = change in stress/change in strain = E. A steeper stress-strain line means larger E and a stiffer material. Always check the axes before interpreting steepness.

figure.purpose: Teach graph construction and gradient meaning
figure.brief: Stress-strain axes with two straight material lines, a large gradient triangle, and a shaded proportional region only.
figure.alt_text: Two stress-strain gradients compare Young moduli in the proportional region.

blocks.title: Calculate E from a wire
content: A wire has L = 2.00 m, A = 4.00 × 10⁻⁷ m², F = 80.0 N and ΔL = 2.00 mm = 2.00 × 10⁻³ m.
Independent check: stress = 2.00 × 10⁸ Pa and strain = 1.00 × 10⁻³, so stress/strain = 2.00 × 10¹¹ Pa.

figure.purpose: Teach complete substitution and second-route check
figure.brief: Two-column worked layout: direct FL/(AΔL) route and separate stress/strain route reaching the same E.
figure.alt_text: Two independent calculation routes give the same Young modulus.

blocks.title: Young modulus is not spring constant
content: Spring constant k describes an object and depends on its material and dimensions. Young modulus E compares stress with strain and characterises the material in the proportional region.
Two wires of the same material may have different k because their lengths or areas differ, while their Young modulus is the same under the model.

figure.purpose: Separate object stiffness from material stiffness
figure.brief: Comparison table with columns spring constant k and Young modulus E, showing dependence on dimensions only under k.
figure.alt_text: Spring constant and Young modulus are contrasted as object and material stiffness measures.

blocks.title: Choose the shortest route
content: If stress and strain are given, use E = stress/strain. If F, L, A and ΔL are given, use E = FL/(AΔL). If a stress-strain graph is given, use its proportional gradient.
Keep the proportional-region condition visible. Designing the wire experiment and managing measurement uncertainty belong to Lesson 6.

misconceptions_addressed: steeper means stiffer without checking axes
skills_students_can_now_use: calculate Young modulus from stress and strain
calculate E from F, L, A and ΔL
next_lesson_can_assume: E is tensile stress divided by tensile strain
stress-strain gradient equals E in proportional region
